claims.text: As-synthesized high-entropy or multi-component concentrated alloys possess local lattice distortions and chemical short-range order.
Local lattice distortions and chemical short-range order significantly enhance yield strength relative to a processed state in which both features are reduced.
Local lattice distortions and chemical short-range order significantly enhance work hardening relative to a processed state in which both features are reduced.
A post-synthesis thermal or mechanical treatment can reduce lattice distortions and short-range order while preserving overall composition and grain size.
Dislocation-mediated plasticity is dominant during room-temperature testing at moderate strain rates.
Lattice distortion and chemical ordering create an uneven local energy landscape.
The energy landscape produced by lattice distortion and chemical ordering raises barriers to dislocation nucleation and glide.
Increased resistance to dislocation motion raises yield strength.
Dislocation impediment promotes a higher work-hardening rate.
The untreated alloy should have higher yield strength than the annealed control.
The untreated alloy should exhibit more pronounced work hardening than the annealed control.
The untreated alloy should show more dislocation interactions with local structural inhomogeneities than the processed control.
The proposed lattice-distortion and short-range-order mechanism is dominant at moderate temperatures and strain rates.
At extreme temperatures or very high strain rates, twinning or dynamic phase transformations may overshadow the proposed mechanism.
The relative contributions of lattice distortion and chemical ordering to strength have not been isolated.
The quantitative effects of lattice distortion and chemical ordering may vary with composition and processing history.

Failure to observe a statistically significant reduction in both yield strength and work-hardening rate after processing, or observation of higher processed-state strength, would falsify the hypothesis.
